blocks.x: I arrived at Palace Merano, the storied wellness getaway in South Tyrol near the Italian Dolomites, utterly famished. After an early-morning flight to Venice, followed by a four-hour drive, I want to collapse in bed almost as much as I want a snack. Once I get to my room I’m dreaming of raiding the mini bar or devouring a complimentary fruit basket when I look around to see—nothing. No nectarines or oranges or grapes, no tray of sweets; I thrust open the doors of the armoire, but all I see is a large bottle of mineral water and a selection of caffeine-free herbal teas. There’s even no coffee machine, let alone coffee.

I take a deep breath, reminding myself that this must be part of what I signed up for: Palace Merano’s Revital Method, the house detox protocol overseen by Dr. Massimiliano Mayrhofer, the scientific director and a physician of regenerative medicine. The program aims to boost each participant’s physical and mental performance while slowing the aging process. The Palace is usually booked out in winter by regulars who have been coming here to detox for decades; a four-day program starts at $3,900, excluding the room (and climbs from there depending on duration, accommodation, and the time of year).

blocks.x: The Belle Epoque-style Palace Merano hotel, set in a valley amidst the snow-capped Dolomites, was initially constructed in 1906 to serve aristocrats that flocked here at the turn of the century.

As with every guest who arrives, my first appointment is with one of the Palace’s medical staff. Dr. Sabrina Ebner walks me through what my next five days will look like: morning acupuncture, hydrotherapy, and massage treatments, followed by specialty appointments in the afternoons. We discuss my detox goals, which mostly amount to undoing a summer of wine, pasta, and UV rays.

But the reason I’m really here is the Palace’s neuro-wellness offerings. At my request she adds cognitive testing to my schedule, along with a body composition scan. She gives me a small brown binder that I’ll hand to every practitioner I see, so they can catalog my journey. I fan open the pages and review my week ahead, and I’m relieved to see there’s no mandatory sunrise breath work, ecstatic dance classes, or group intention-setting circles. Only the classics, and all optional: pilates, yoga, and morning meditations.

My morning treatments are the most luxurious part of my day, but the cognitive sessions are what really help me learn more about my mind and body. My grandmother had Alzheimer’s disease, and by the end of her battle was vacant. I watched what her long, slow decline cost her, my father, and my aunt. The wellness industry has reoriented itself around longevity, and brain health is naturally a part of that. But I’m not just interested in getting more years out of this life; I’m interested in how to be at my best—neurologically—as I age.

What to expect from a neuro-wellness retreat

The Palace's isn’t the kind of neuro-wellness detox where you surrender your phone at check-in and rediscover your inner world without technology: Sure, I do use my phone less, and I never open my computer. But the actual neurological work here is diagnostic—I’m not unplugging per se; instead I’m gaining information.

While mindfulness is naturally part of the detox, there is no pressure to participate in collective rituals or follow a predefined spiritual path, practices that are increasingly common at wellness hotels. This makes me feel eat ease, and as I move through the property I notice a similar calm among fellow guests, many of whom are traveling alone. It seems we all have the space and freedom to embark on a highly personal journey, retreating at our own pace.
